claims.claim: Social workers help individuals, groups, families, and communities prevent and cope with problems in everyday life; typical duties include identifying people who need help, assessing needs, strengths and support networks, connecting clients to community resources, responding to crises such as child abuse and mental health emergencies, following up, and maintaining case records.

BLS counted about 810,900 social work jobs in 2024, distributed as roughly 399,900 child, family, and school social workers; 193,200 healthcare social workers; 136,800 mental health and substance abuse social workers; and 81,000 social workers, all other. The median annual wage was $61,330 in May 2024, and employment is projected to grow 6 percent from 2024 to 2034.

The largest employers of social workers in 2024 were individual and family services (17 percent), local government excluding education and hospitals (14 percent), state government excluding education and hospitals (12 percent), and educational services, state, local and private (9 percent).

Healthcare social workers help clients understand a diagnosis and adjust housing or care and may specialize in geriatric social work, hospice and palliative care, or medical social work; BLS projects growth in mental health and substance abuse social work partly because people with drug offenses may be directed to treatment programs as a supplement or occasional alternative to incarceration.

Social and human service assistants are a distinct occupation: about 449,600 jobs in 2024, median annual wage $45,120 in May 2024, typical entry-level education a high school diploma or equivalent with short-term on-the-job training, working under the direction of social workers, psychologists, or other community and social service workers, under titles such as case work aide, family service assistant, and human service worker.

Community health workers are a separate BLS occupation with about 65,100 jobs in 2024, a median annual wage of $51,030 in May 2024, typical entry-level education of a high school diploma, and projected growth of 11 percent from 2024 to 2034; their titles vary by community served, including community health representatives in Tribal communities, promotores de la salud in Spanish-speaking communities, and peer support specialists in recovery roles.

A bachelor's degree in social work is the most common requirement for entry-level nonclinical social worker positions; clinical social workers typically need an MSW, which generally takes two years and includes a supervised practicum. A BSW is not required for MSW admission, and some programs let BSW graduates complete an MSW in less than two years. All accredited BSW programs require supervised fieldwork or an internship.

The Council on Social Work Education, Board of Accreditation is a CHEA-recognized programmatic accrediting body that accredits baccalaureate, master's, and practice doctorate professional social work education degree programs within the United States and its territories (recognition record dated 2025).

Practice doctorate programs, most of which award the DSW, prepare practitioner-scholars to advance and innovate practice at micro, mezzo, and/or macro levels and in professional leadership or teaching; CSWE states that it neither addresses nor designates a terminal degree for social work education or practice. Research doctorates are not within CSWE's practice-doctorate accreditation scope.

Licensure of social workers in the United States is set by each state: all states require clinical social workers to be licensed, some states also require a license or credential for nonclinical social workers, clinical licensure requires an accredited master's degree plus post-graduate supervised clinical experience whose length varies by state and a passing clinical examination, and specific titles vary by state.

The Association of Social Work Boards develops and administers social work licensing examinations at four levels - Bachelors, Masters, Advanced Generalist, and Clinical - for member boards in the United States and Canada; candidates apply for licensure with their state or provincial board, which grants the license, before registering for the exam.

New York Education Law defines licensed master social work (assessment, counseling, case management, supervision other than clinical supervision, and clinical practice under supervision in authorized settings) and licensed clinical social work (adding diagnosis of mental and behavioral disorders, psychotherapy, and treatment planning), which documents that a state can draw legally distinct master's-level and clinical scopes.

New York Education Law section 7706 bars other named licensed health professionals from using the titles 'licensed clinical social worker' or 'licensed master social worker' unless licensed under that article, and exempts a range of activities - including screening, assessment, referral, non-clinical service planning, case management, and peer services - that unlicensed staff may perform, with restricted activities such as diagnosis and psychotherapy remaining with licensed professionals. This is one state's version of a pattern that varies across jurisdictions.

Clinical social workers are licensed to diagnose and treat mental, behavioral, and emotional disorders and provide individual, group, family, and couples therapy; macro social work, by contrast, works at a broad level with community organizations and policymakers to develop or improve social programs, services, and conditions. Advocacy with and on behalf of clients is part of the occupation's own description of itself.

Generalist practice applies prevention and intervention methods at individual (micro), group (mezzo), and community (macro) levels; mezzo practice includes task, therapy, education, self-help, support, and psychoeducation groups, and macro practice addresses citywide, state, or national social problems, often from nonprofits, government departments, and human rights organizations.

The National Association of Social Workers describes the profession's historic and defining feature as a dual focus on individual wellbeing in a social context and the wellbeing of society, with attention to environmental forces that create, contribute to, and address problems in living, and names six core values: service, social justice, dignity and worth of the person, importance of human relationships, integrity, and competence. Its listed professional activities span direct practice, community organizing, supervision, consultation, administration, advocacy, social and political action, policy development, education, and research.

New York Education Law section 6513 makes unauthorized use of a professional title regulated under that title a class A misdemeanor, and knowingly aiding or employing three or more unauthorized title users a class E felony, which is the general mechanism by which protected professional titles are enforced in that state.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many licensure categories exist and what they are called.
positions: ASWB publishes four examination categories (Bachelors, Masters, Advanced Generalist, Clinical), which many summaries then present as four national license types with fixed names such as LBSW, LMSW, LCSW.
BLS states that specific titles and requirements vary by state, and New York's statute uses only two categories (LMSW and LCSW).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the four ASWB exam categories as exam categories only, states plainly that licenses are granted by state boards and that titles and requirements vary, and uses New York as an explicitly labelled single-state example. No national license-name taxonomy or hour count is asserted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a doctorate is the terminal or expected degree in social work.
positions: Marketing-oriented sources frequently frame the DSW or PhD as the profession's terminal degree.
CSWE states that it neither addresses nor designates a terminal degree for social work education or practice.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows CSWE and describes doctoral study as a specialization split between practice (DSW) and research (PhD) routes, with the MSW as the practice degree most advanced roles rest on.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether human-service assistants are simply less-qualified social workers.
positions: Common shorthand treats all agency helping staff as 'social workers'.

BLS tracks social and human service assistants and community health workers as separate occupations with their own entry requirements, and New York's statute defines specific activities unlicensed staff may perform.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats them as distinct occupations with different scope rather than a hierarchy of competence, and says so explicitly.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive factual claims at all - only template text ('is a foundational concept in Social Work & Human Services', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') with no sources, no occupational content, and no mention of degrees, licensure, settings, or practice levels.
The draft's vocabulary entry defined the topic title as 'A foundational Social Work & Human Services concept covered in this lesson', which is circular and carries no information.
The draft's three quick-check items tested generic study skills rather than any social work content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with researched content: occupational duties and settings, 2024 employment and May 2024 wage figures, degree pathways, accreditation scope, licensure structure, title protection, clinical vs macro practice, and the micro/mezzo/macro frame.
Dated every quantitative figure to its BLS reference period (2024 employment, May 2024 wages, 2024-34 projections) rather than presenting them as undated facts.
Scoped all licensure statements to U.S. state jurisdiction and used New York only as a labelled example, rather than describing any one state's rules as universal.
Replaced the draft's four generic vocabulary terms with ten field-specific, non-circular definitions.
Rebuilt the question bank as five sourced items testing occupational, regulatory, and conceptual content, and added an analogy-limits statement the draft lacked.

Verification pass correction: an earlier draft said New York Education Law section 7706 reserves the social work titles generally. Section 7706 in fact bars other enumerated licensed health professionals from using them; general title protection comes from section 6513, which makes unauthorized use of any regulated professional title a class A misdemeanor. Both the lesson text and the corresponding question were rewritten and section 6513 was added to the source records.
rightsIssues: The NASW Code of Ethics is copyrighted. It is recorded here as REFERENCE_ONLY; the lesson describes the preamble's dual-focus framing and names the six core values in original wording and reproduces none of its text.

BLS text, charts, and tables are in the public domain with credit requested, but photographs on BLS pages are licensed from stock providers and were not used. BLS also blocks automated retrieval as a matter of usage policy; the two OOH profiles were read through Internet Archive snapshots (June 2026 and July 2026) of the same public-domain pages rather than by scraping bls.gov, and the figures cited carry BLS's own 2024 / May 2024 reference dates.

The Mavs Open Press OER text is licensed CC BY-NC 4.0. Because the NonCommercial condition may not suit this project's distribution, it is recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording from it was adapted; it supports the micro/mezzo/macro framing only.
New York Education Law is a state edict of government and is not subject to copyright; its provisions are summarized rather than quoted at length.
CSWE, CHEA, and ASWB pages are copyrighted organizational content recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY; facts were synthesized and prose written fresh.

sourceRecords.title: New York Education Law Section 7706 - Exempt persons
sourceRecords.provider: New York State Legislature (via NY Senate legislation portal)
sourceRecords.notes: Documented single-state example of title protection plus scope exemptions: the titles licensed clinical social worker and licensed master social worker are reserved to persons licensed under the article, while unlicensed staff may perform screening, assessment, referral, non-clinical service planning, case management, and peer services, with diagnosis and psychotherapy restricted. Used to ground the social work / human services scope distinction in actual law and explicitly labelled in the lesson as one state's rules.

sourceRecords.provider: New York State Legislature (via NY Senate legislation portal)
